notes:
Context dump covering T193 (M4a acceptance) and T215 (key_byte call-site sweep). Four categories below.

=== (1) HYPOTHESES FORMED AND RULED OUT ===

H1: A3 colour-inversion violations might be caused by a bug in flipColex or the colex colour-inversion mapping.
  RULED OUT by: all A3 violations had ko=16 (KO_NONE) and the inverted L/H values were +16/+16 or -16/-16 — the values of the opponent's empty-board root, not a colour-flip error. The pattern was wrong-values-at-right-colex, not wrong-colex.

H2: A9 entry sort violations might be an off-by-one in the accept.zig entry_offset computation (byte offset vs entry index confusion).
  RULED OUT by: tracing readGroupIndex — entry_offset is entry_cumulative (an entry count, not byte count), and every access multiplies by WZO2_ENTRY_SIZE. The computation is correct. The violations are real sort-order defects in the artifact, not a reader bug.

H3: The T193 bug might also exist in the consumer_load.zig builder (3×3 path).
  RULED OUT by: consumer_load.zig:289 correctly passes 1 for passes. Also, the 3×3 artifact passes all four M4a checks cleanly. The bug was 4×4-only.

H4: There might be a second literal-swap defect at another encodeKeyByte call site (the premise of T215).
  RULED OUT by: T215 sweep of all five production call sites. Every literal matches its loop context. The T193 fix was the sole defect of this class.

=== (2) HAZARDS, SMELLS, FRAGILE ASSUMPTIONS ===

HAZARD 1 — Threaded I/O in util.zig corrupts stdout on non-zero exit.
  util.out() uses std.Io.Threaded (util.zig:17-26), which spawns a background I/O thread. When the process calls std.process.exit(1), the thread does not get joined and stdout buffers are only partially flushed. Observed behavior: writing stdout to file with '>' produced truncated/corrupted output (lines missing characters, e.g. 'sorted=true' → 'orted=true'). Writing with 'tee' or '2>&1' to a pipe worked because both streams share a fd. This cost ~20 minutes of T193. Any tool using util.out() that exits non-zero may produce silently corrupt evidence stdout files. Not investigated: whether this is a Zig std.Io.Threaded bug, a missing finalization step in the accept tool, or an inherent limitation of the pattern.

HAZARD 2 — Duplicate encodeKeyByte with divergent types.
  artifact2.zig:60 has encodeKeyByte(side: u1, ko: u8, passes: u1, terminal: u1, ko_bits: u8). oracle_v2_accept.zig:121 has encodeKeyByte(side: u1, ko_point: u8, passes: u2, terminal: bool, ko_bits: u8). The bit layouts are currently identical (both shift passes by 2+ko_bits, both OR terminal into bit 0), but the different types mask the duplication — a reviewer would not notice these are the same function. If the canonical encoder's bit layout changes, the accept tool must change in lockstep, and the compiler will not flag the divergence because the types differ. SPECULATION: this duplication likely arose because the accept tool was written against the spec (which uses 'passes: u2' in prose) while artifact2.zig was written with the tighter u1 type. Not investigated: how the duplication came to be.

HAZARD 3 — artifact2.lookup() accepts passes: u2 but @intCast's to u1 internally.
  If a caller passes passes=2 (which is a valid u2 value), the @intCast panics in safe builds or silently truncates to 0 in fast builds. The sole current caller (gtp.zig:bounds2) guards passes >= 2 before calling, so no live defect. But the u2 signature overstates the function's capability and invites misuse. SPECULATION: the u2 type was used because gtp.zig represents passes as u2 for the passes=2 terminal shortcut; the lookup function matched that type rather than enforcing its own constraint.

HAZARD 4 — Two different terminal-flag construction patterns.
  oracle_v2_build.zig (4×4) builds all entries with terminal=0, then patches terminal flags in a separate Phase 3b via the same iteration order. oracle_v2_consumer_load.zig (3×3) computes terminal inline during row construction. Both are correct, but the two-phase approach in build.zig is fragile: Phase 3b must iterate entries in the exact same order as Phase 3, otherwise terminal flags land on the wrong entries. The order is identical (ko-major, side-minor for passes=0; then passes=1), but this is guaranteed only by code duplication, not by a shared iterator. A future change to one phase that forgets the other would produce silently wrong terminal bits. Not investigated: whether a test would catch this.

SMELL 1 — passes: u1 type enables the literal-swap bug class.
  Every builder uses literal 0 or 1 for passes. Both are valid u1 values. The compiler cannot distinguish 'passes=0 for the passes=0 loop' from 'passes=0 for the passes=1 loop.' A named enum Passes { zero, one } would have caught T193 at compile time. This was noted in T215 §3.3 but not remedied — that is a follow-up task.

FRAGILE ASSUMPTION — The 4×4 WZO2 artifact tested in T193 is the T192 build.
  I assumed untracked/oracle-v2/oracle-4x4-v2.wzo2 (timestamp Aug 1 11:03, 518,123,097 bytes) was produced by T192's re-run with the 64MiB chunk fix. But no T192 evidence file exists in docs/evidence/ORACLE-V2/ — only the T192 brief (untracked/T192-wzo2-oom-fix.md) and the T184 OOM report. The artifact's embedded SHA-256 matches its own hash, but I did not verify it was built from the commit with the 64MiB chunk fix (as opposed to being a pre-fix artifact that happened to not OOM). The T184 OOM report says 'No .wzo2 file was written,' so the artifact at 11:03 is plausibly the T192 re-run. But this is an assumption, not a verification.

=== (3) UNCERTAINTIES IN DELIVERABLES ===

T193 uncertainty — A5 stride=97 samples only ~1% of 99M entries.
  I would not defend that A5 passing at 1% sampling proves the round-trip is correct for all entries. The sample is at a fixed stride (every 97th entry), which means it covers entries from different groups at different positions. A systematic error affecting entries at a specific position within groups (e.g., the last entry of every group) would be missed if 97 does not hit that position. I did not verify that the stride is coprime to every group size.

T193 uncertainty — I did not independently verify the A3 violation count.
  The accept tool reported 16,314,978 colour-inversion violations. I took this number on trust. I did not manually verify a sample of violations to confirm the root-cause diagnosis. The pattern in the first 10 violations (all ko=16, L/H values consistent with wrong-passes collision) is strong evidence, but I did not check whether there are ALSO A3 violations with ko≠16 that would indicate a different root cause.

T215 uncertainty — I did not inspect the consumer_load.zig 2×2/3×2 paths.
  The sweep covered consumer_load.zig's 3×3 builder path (confirmed correct). I did not verify whether consumer_load.zig also builds 2×2 or 3×2 artifacts, or whether those paths have their own encodeKeyByte call sites. The grep identified only two production call sites in that file, both in what I identified as the 3×3 path. If there are additional builder functions, they were not audited.

T215 uncertainty — decodeKeyByte has no production callers, but I only grepped for the function name.
  It is possible that some code destructures key bytes manually (bit shifts + masks) without calling decodeKeyByte. I did not audit the full codebase for manual key-byte destructuring. gtp.zig uses artifact2.lookup() which scans entries without decoding, so the risk is low, but I did not exhaustively verify there is no other reader.

=== (4) WHAT MISLED OR COST TIME ===

COST 1 — Threaded I/O stdout corruption (T193).
  The AGENTS.md rule 'stdout = data, stderr = diagnostics' implies they can be separated. But util.out() uses std.Io.Threaded which corrupts stdout when stderr is suppressed (2>/dev/null) and the process exits non-zero. I tried three approaches before discovering that '2>&1 | tee' works. The util.zig implementation was not obvious — I had to trace the stdoutWriter function to discover the threaded I/O. This is a tooling defect that will hit every task that produces evidence stdout.

COST 2 — T193 brief said 'Commit stdout + verdicts' but the stdout capture was fragile.
  The brief did not warn about the threaded I/O issue. The build-T184-2026-08-01.stdout file in the same directory is 170 lines, which suggests the builder (which exits 0 on success) does not have this problem — only tools that exit non-zero trigger it.

COST 3 — I initially read T215 as 'fix any bugs found' rather than 'read-only audit.'
  The brief says 'Read-only audit' at the top, but the urgency framing ('costs another full build plus another acceptance run') and the instruction 'If you find a live defect, say so at the top of the file and stop' suggested action. I applied the T193 fix during T193 (correctly), and T215 found nothing else to fix. But the framing created a moment of hesitation about whether 'read-only' included applying fixes if found.
